headline.title: Washington quietly signs its AI order as enterprise AI's next wave breaks.
headline.summary: President Trump quietly signed a watered-down AI executive order this week — voluntary testing, no licensing — even as OpenAI and Microsoft unveiled dueling visions for enterprise AI's next phase. Anthropic widened access to its powerful Mythos cyber model while warning that a public release still needs safeguards that don't yet exist.

source_headlines.title: Trump's AI executive order is signed quietly, with voluntary testing and no licensing
Anthropic expands Mythos access to 150 partners via Project Glasswing as public launch slips
Microsoft Build debuts seven in-house models, MAI Thinking 1, and Frontier Tuning
OpenAI recasts Codex for all knowledge work: report, annotations, role plugins, sites
SK Hynix to double memory-chip capacity as the AI token crunch bites
Uber caps employee AI token spending at $1,500 per month
Historian Jürgen Kocka on Luddites, capitalism and whether AI breaks the old pattern

stories.title: Washington signs its AI order in private, with no teeth.
stories.toc_summary: Trump signed an AI executive order substantially identical to the draft he scrapped two weeks ago — voluntary testing, a 30-day pre-release window, and an explicit ban on mandatory licensing.
stories.quick_take: After pulling a high-profile signing ceremony at the eleventh hour, President Trump quietly signed an AI executive order this week that is substantially the same as the draft scrapped a fortnight earlier [1]. It makes safety testing voluntary, shortens the pre-release model-sharing window from 90 to 30 days, names the NSA as lead tester, and stands up a Treasury-run cybersecurity clearinghouse [1]. A new disclaimer expressly forbids any mandatory licensing or pre-clearance regime [1]. The catalyst, ironically, was the cyber capability of Anthropic's Mythos model [1].

bullets.label: What changed:
bullets.text: The only material edit from the scrapped draft is the pre-release sharing window dropping from 90 to 30 days — the 90-day version had drawn the loudest industry backlash for slowing release cycles [1].

bullets.label: Who blinked:
bullets.text: Former AI czar David Sacks reportedly called Trump hours before the original ceremony to talk him out of signing; Trump said he feared it would hand China an edge in the AI race [1].

bullets.label: Odd-bedfellow reactions:
bullets.text: Dean Ball called it 'teeing up the infrastructure for a model licensing regime'; Steve Bannon vowed to push toward mandatory testing 'one bite at a time'; Bernie Sanders dismissed it as nearly toothless [1].

bullets.label: Net effect:
bullets.text: Analysts note the order largely formalizes what labs already do voluntarily, leaving the real fight to speculation about what comes next [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: The signing turns an informal arrangement into a written process — and both the safety camp and the acceleration camp now read that process as a foothold to expand or contain. The disclaimer says no licensing today; the politics suggest the next move is already being fought over [1].

stories.title: Anthropic widens Mythos access even as a public launch slips.
stories.toc_summary: Project Glasswing now puts Anthropic's most powerful cyber model in the hands of 150 new partners across 15 countries — but the broad public release is being pushed back for want of safeguards.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic expanded access to its Mythos model under Project Glasswing, adding 150 partners across 15 countries and new sectors — energy, water, communications, healthcare and computer hardware [1]. The common thread: organizations where a successful attack on the codebase could affect more than 100 million people [1]. Yet Anthropic walked back its 'coming weeks' timeline for a public release, saying it first needs robust safeguards that it — and, to its knowledge, every other developer — has yet to build [1].

bullets.label: Why these partners:
bullets.text: Anthropic says each partner shares one trait — a breach of their systems could be catastrophic at national or global scale [1].

bullets.label: The cost problem:
bullets.text: Testers told The Information that Mythos is 'eye-wateringly expensive,' burning through millions of dollars in tokens quickly — and Anthropic is still subsidizing usage [1].

bullets.label: Worth it anyway:
bullets.text: Despite the bill, firms are reportedly realigning budgets to build strategy around Mythos for when it becomes broadly available [1].

bullets.label: Mixed messaging:
bullets.text: The walk-back from the Opus 4.8 launch's 'next couple of weeks' to 'safeguards that don't exist yet' echoes the confusion around the government's own executive order [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Mythos is both the catalyst for Washington's executive order and the model Anthropic says it can't yet release safely. The gap between 'powerful enough to reshape cyber' and 'safe enough to ship' is now the industry's defining tension [1].

stories.title: Microsoft ships seven in-house models and a cheaper frontier.
stories.toc_summary: At Build, Microsoft unveiled seven home-grown models led by the one-trillion-parameter MAI Thinking 1, plus Frontier Tuning — betting on tunable, low-cost models over raw benchmark supremacy.
stories.quick_take: Microsoft used Build to unveil seven in-house models — Image 2.5, Image 2.5 Flash, Transcribe 1.5, Thinking 1, Voice 2, Voice 2 Flash and Code 1 Flash [1]. The headliner, MAI Thinking 1, is a roughly one-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model trained with zero synthetic data or distillation [1]. Its agentic-coding benchmarks trail rivals, but observers note Microsoft is playing a different game: cost and distribution, not raw state-of-the-art [1].

bullets.label: Built from scratch:
bullets.text: Commentators credited Mustafa Suleyman with standing up a full 'neolab' inside Microsoft in two years — controlling the stack from chip to model to harness [1].

bullets.label: Frontier Tuning:
bullets.text: Enterprises can tune custom, company-specific agents; tuned for McKinsey's tasks, MAI delivered the highest win rate, beating GPT-5.5 on quality at 10x lower cost [1].

bullets.label: Nadella's framing:
bullets.text: The CEO called it a shift from 'consuming a Frontier model to fully participating at the Frontier' [1].

bullets.label: The catch:
bullets.text: Few outsiders have hands-on access, and Thinking 1's scores on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and SWE-bench Pro lag even last-generation rivals — so the bet rests on tuning economics, not leaderboards [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: With the strongest enterprise distribution of any vendor, Microsoft doesn't need to win benchmarks — it needs models cheap and tunable enough to deploy at scale. That makes MAI a serious play even if no one fires up Thinking 1 over GPT-5.5 [1].

stories.title: OpenAI recasts Codex as the interface for all knowledge work.
stories.toc_summary: Codex hit 5 million weekly users — growing fastest among non-developers — as OpenAI added annotations, role-specific plugins and shareable 'sites' to push it beyond coding.
stories.quick_take: Alongside a report titled 'The Next Era of Knowledge Work,' OpenAI revealed Codex has reached 5 million weekly active users, with non-technical knowledge workers adopting it three times faster than developers [1]. New features include annotations (highlighting parts of an artifact for the model), role-specific plugins, and 'sites' that turn any Codex artifact into a shareable website or web app [1]. Roughly half of users now run parallel tasks, up from under a third in mid-April [1].

bullets.label: The thesis:
bullets.text: OpenAI argues knowledge work is 'still waiting for its factory redesign,' bottlenecked by three frictions: finding inputs, coordination, and approvals [1].

bullets.label: Role plugins:
bullets.text: Six new function bundles — sales, data analytics, creative production, product design, public equity investing and investment banking — package 62 apps and 110 skills, productizing best practices per role [1].

bullets.label: Sites:
bullets.text: Described as 'Claude artifacts on steroids,' sites let anyone build, deploy and share disposable web apps — examples include a revenue-forecast planner and an event-ops dashboard [1].

bullets.label: Parallel work:
bullets.text: The shift from sequential to parallel tasks, the report says, lets a single worker operate at the scale of a small team [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: OpenAI is betting that building disposable websites and web apps becomes a core knowledge-work primitive — as routine as a slide deck or spreadsheet. If it's right, the interface for knowledge work is up for grabs, and Codex is making its claim [1].

stories.title: SK Hynix doubles down on memory as the token crunch bites.
stories.toc_summary: SK Hynix will double memory-chip capacity by decade's end, treating AI demand as structural — but warns the shortage could persist until 2030.
stories.quick_take: Facing a memory bottleneck in the AI supply chain, SK Hynix plans to double its memory-chip manufacturing capacity [1]. High-bandwidth memory prices for AI servers have more than doubled this year, and manufacturers had been reluctant to build new plants after past cycles punished long-term investment [1]. SK Hynix's move signals it now sees AI-driven demand as a structural change rather than a passing spike [1].

bullets.label: The timeline:
bullets.text: The doubling targets the end of the decade, so it won't ease the near-term crunch — the chairman said the shortage could last until 2030 [1].

bullets.label: Why now:
bullets.text: Surging token usage has rippled shortages across the AI supply chain, with memory among the most acute [1].

bullets.label: Breaking the cycle:
bullets.text: Historically, chip-price cyclicality deterred new plants that risked missing peak demand; SK Hynix is betting that calculus has changed [1].

bullets.label: The principle:
bullets.text: The chairman argued the whole AI industry must become more sustainable, since sudden price jumps ultimately hurt [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: The subsidy era of cheap AI is giving way to a scarcity era defined by physical limits — compute, power, and now memory. Capacity decisions made today set the ceiling on what agentic AI can do for years [1].

stories.title: Uber puts a $1,500 monthly cap on each employee's AI tokens.
stories.toc_summary: Uber has capped AI token spending at $1,500 per employee per month — a sign that cost management is becoming a defining vector of enterprise AI.
stories.quick_take: Uber has imposed a $1,500 monthly cap on AI token spending across all employees [1]. The move makes the ride-hailing firm an emblem of the shifting economics of agentic AI, where rising per-seat costs force companies to ration usage [1]. It underscores the brief's central theme: the next wave of enterprise AI is as much about cost control as capability [1].

bullets.label: The signal:
bullets.text: As workloads move from assisted to agentic, token consumption climbs — and finance teams are starting to put hard ceilings on it [1].

bullets.label: Part of a pattern:
bullets.text: Uber has repeatedly surfaced as 'exhibit A' in coverage of the changing economics of agentic AI [1].

bullets.label: The tension:
bullets.text: Caps risk throttling exactly the parallel, high-token workflows that make agentic tools valuable [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If your team is scaling agentic tools, model the per-seat token economics now — the era of unmetered AI spend is ending, and budgets are becoming the binding constraint [1].

stories.title: A top historian asks whether AI finally breaks the old pattern.
stories.toc_summary: Historian Jürgen Kocka brings 200 years of industrial history to the AI debate — arguing the job apocalypse never came before, but conceding this time the pace could outrun renewal.
stories.quick_take: On Everlast, capitalism historian Jürgen Kocka argues that the catastrophic job losses feared in past technological shifts never materialized — individual tasks vanished, but rarely whole professions, and new needs and jobs always emerged [1]. The Luddites, he notes, were not primarily anti-technology; they fought for social embedding and a share of the gains [1]. Yet he concedes that AI compressing 'a century into a decade' could, this time, outrun creative renewal — though he stresses such forecasts are notoriously unreliable [1].

bullets.label: Creative destruction:
bullets.text: Invoking Schumpeter, Kocka frames innovation as always producing winners and losers — the task of politics is to make the gains dominate the harms [1].

bullets.label: Against accelerationism:
bullets.text: He rejects the Silicon Valley view (Nick Land, Marc Andreessen) that AI is merely capitalism's logical endpoint, arguing it ignores the passions, family and values that techno-utopias never capture [1].

bullets.label: Invention vs. diffusion:
bullets.text: Even Jobs, Watt and Einstein worked within collective structures — though individuals can still amass enormous power, as Musk and Trump show [1].

bullets.label: The closing counsel:
bullets.text: Ambivalence and uncertainty are historical norms, Kocka says, but individual agency endures — realism plus courage over fatalism [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The historian's lens cuts both the doom and the hype: the decisive variable in the AI transition isn't the technology but its social and political embedding — and whether renewal can keep pace with disruption [1].

editorial.title: Vegetables, quietly eaten.
editorial.intro: Two threads braided through today's news: a government doing the minimum it can still call action, and an industry colliding with the physics of its own success.
editorial.body: The executive order Washington finally signed was, by the administration's own body language, vegetables — eaten in private, with no ceremony, after a louder version was yanked at the last minute. It formalizes what labs already do and forbids what critics feared, leaving everyone to argue about a future that hasn't been written. The real action, meanwhile, is economic. OpenAI and Microsoft spent the day describing the same shift from opposite ends: OpenAI reimagining the interface of knowledge work through Codex sites and plugins, Microsoft attacking its cost through tunable in-house models. Anthropic's Mythos sits at the center of both stories — powerful enough to trigger federal policy, expensive enough to burn millions in tokens, and, by Anthropic's own admission, not yet safe enough to ship widely. SK Hynix's capacity bet and Uber's spending cap are two faces of one coin: the subsidy era of cheap, abundant AI is ending, and scarcity — of memory, of compute, of budget — is becoming the organizing constraint.
editorial.pull_quote: The subsidy era of AI is ending; scarcity is becoming the organizing principle.
editorial.outro: And beneath the launches, a historian's reminder: every prior wave of automation provoked the same fears, and the same fears were mostly wrong — but 'mostly' is not 'always', and the pace this time is unlike anything in the record.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: The next phase of enterprise AI will be won not on benchmarks but on economics — on who can make capability cheap, tunable, and shippable at scale.
